explanations.answer: So His ways are known on earth
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. Right after the blessing ask, the song says "…that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." (Psalm 67:2). The blessing isn't the finish line. The song ties it to His ways being known. Think of it like a cookie box: it's made to be passed around, not hoarded in the pantry.

explanations.answer: So their land is safe from war
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, because blessing and safety feel like they go together. But the song never mentions war. It says the blessing is "…that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." (Psalm 67:2). Everything in the song points outward, toward the nations.

explanations.answer: So they can rest from hard work
explanations.explanation: Rest sounds lovely, and I'd sign up for a nap myself. But the song doesn't say a word about rest or work. It says the blessing is "…that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." (Psalm 67:2). That's the reason the song gives, friend.

Yes, friend! The chorus says, "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You." (Psalm 67:3). Say it twice and it sounds like the song really means it. That's a big circle of voices, and nobody's left out of the line.

Good guess, friend. But this chorus never mentions priests. It says, "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You." (Psalm 67:3). The invitation is wide open, wider than any one group.

Singers and a song, I see the connection! But the chorus doesn't name singers at all. It says, "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You." (Psalm 67:3). The song hands the microphone to everybody.

Justly, friend! The song says the nations can be glad "…for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). That's a real reason to sing. When the Judge is just, joy makes sense.
Harshly is a rough word, and the song doesn't use it. It says God judges the peoples "justly" (Psalm 67:4). That's why the nations can be glad and sing for joy.
Rarely would be a strange reason to sing! The song says "…You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). The word is "justly," and that's the reason for the joy.

That's it, friend. The verse says, "…for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). So the nations get a Judge and a Leader. I'd follow that guide way before I'd follow my own sense of direction.

Scattering is a pretty scary picture, and the song doesn't paint it. It says, "…for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). Leading is the word, and the verse right before it calls the nations to be glad and sing for joy.

Counting is a fair guess, but it's not in this verse. The song says, "…for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). God leads the nations, and that's the good news in the line.

Right on, friend! The song says, "The earth has yielded its harvest…" (Psalm 67:6). The earth gave something, and the song notices. It's the kind of moment where you look at a full table and just say thank you.
Silver is shiny, but it's not in this song. The verse says, "The earth has yielded its harvest…" (Psalm 67:6). The harvest is what the earth gave.
Springs make sense for a song about the earth, but the verse says something else. It says, "The earth has yielded its harvest…" (Psalm 67:6). Harvest is the gift the song points to.
True, friend! Right after the harvest line comes "God, our God, blesses us." (Psalm 67:6). The two lines sit side by side. The song hands us the harvest and the blessing in one breath.

It's actually true, friend. Right after "The earth has yielded its harvest…" the song says, "God, our God, blesses us." (Psalm 67:6). The two lines come back to back. Easy one to doubt when the lines go by this fast!

explanations.answer: All the ends of the earth
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. The last line says, "God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him." (Psalm 67:7). The song started with "us" asking for a blessing, and it ends with the whole earth in view. That's a big finish.

Elders are a fair guess in a Bible song, but they're not in this one. The last line says, "God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him." (Psalm 67:7). The song's eyes are on the whole earth.

Kings would make a grand audience, but the song doesn't name them. The last line says, "God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him." (Psalm 67:7). It reaches way past any one kingdom, friend.
